name: Travelers Insurance

profile.address: South 150th Street, Papillion, Sarpy County, Nebraska, 68059
profile.reading:
This data center in Sarpy County, Nebraska, in the La Vista and Papillion area south of Omaha, is a private enterprise facility built and operated by Travelers Insurance, the primary operating subsidiary of The Travelers Companies, a Hartford, Connecticut headquartered property and casualty insurer that traces its roots back to the 19th century and today ranks among the largest insurers in the United States.

Before Travelers publicly confirmed it was the company behind the project, the development moved through local approvals under the code name Project Oasis, a practice large corporations commonly use for major facility construction so that land acquisition and public incentive negotiations are not complicated by a well known corporate name driving up prices or public expectations ahead of time. Once the identity became public, local and national trade coverage, including reporting from Data Center Dynamics, the Omaha World Herald, and Insurance Journal, described the project as a roughly 200 million dollar investment and placed its opening around 2015, part of a broader wave of large scale data center construction that Sarpy County attracted through the 2010s as companies sought sites with available power, favorable tax treatment, and proximity to Omaha's existing fiber and workforce base.

Unlike a colocation or wholesale facility, the Travelers site is not marketed to outside tenants. It exists to run the company's own internal systems, which for a major property and casualty insurer means policy administration platforms, claims processing systems that must remain available around the clock, actuarial and underwriting data, and disaster recovery infrastructure that lets the company keep operating if another facility goes offline, a particularly important consideration for an insurer whose claims volumes can spike sharply after major weather events. Travelers has not published a critical IT load figure in megawatts, total square footage, or a tier certification for the building, which is consistent with how most enterprise owned, single tenant data centers are documented publicly. The parent company discloses what it needs to for local permitting and economic development purposes, in this case largely the investment figure, but treats the technical specifications of a facility supporting its own claims and policy systems as internal operational detail rather than something a competitor or the public needs to see.

profile.facility_note: Opened around 2015, approximately $200M construction cost, developed under the code name Project Oasis before Travelers was publicly named. Located in Sarpy County NE, La Vista/Papillion area south of Omaha.

reading:
Travelers is a property and casualty insurer headquartered in Hartford, Connecticut, and it appears in this registry for the ordinary reason that a large insurer runs its own computing rather than renting it. The registry holds one facility for the company, in Sarpy County, Nebraska, and the stored coordinates fall almost exactly on the parcel the site selection record describes, the south west corner of 144th Street and Schram Road, a short distance north of the village of Springfield in unincorporated Sarpy County.

The project was run under the code name Project Oasis for most of its life, which is why the early Nebraska coverage names no company at all. Travelers was identified publicly in September 2013, at the point the Sarpy County Board was preparing to vote on a development agreement. By then the land had already been rezoned to light industrial and the Sarpy County Economic Development Corporation held an option on it. Site Selection magazine, writing while the project was still being assembled, put the parcel at 140 acres and the building at about 190,000 square feet, and recorded that the search had run nine to ten months from late 2012. Trade coverage of the opening gives the building as roughly 183,000 square feet with 30,000 square feet of raised floor in service and another 30,000 planned, which is the more useful pair of numbers because it separates the shell from the part that actually holds equipment.

The incentive record is unusually explicit for a private data centre. The project qualified under the Nebraska Advantage Act tier written for large data centres, which at the time required a capital investment of at least 200 million dollars and at least 30 new full time employees. In exchange the company received a refund of sales and use taxes on tangible personal property, a sliding scale wage credit, a ten percent investment credit and a personal property tax exemption running up to ten years. Travelers put the investment at 200 million dollars, which is the same number as the threshold, and the job commitment at 30, which is also the threshold. The Omaha Public Power District built a new substation to serve the site, and its willingness to move quickly on power infrastructure was named by the utility as a reason the county won the project.

The building opened in the first half of 2015, with a ribbon cutting attended by the state governor, and it was described at the time as the main hub for the company's data processing, taking over from an older facility at Norcross, Georgia. Construction ran close to two years.

No power figure has been published for this site in any of the four senses that matter. Travelers has not stated a critical IT load. The size of the OPPD service into the building has not been published. There is no public generator count or standby rating, and there is no on site generation. The 200 million dollar figure is capital cost and the 30,000 square feet is raised floor area, and neither converts into megawatts. The facility is private and is not offered for colocation, so there is no marketed capacity to check against either. What is well established is the parcel, the size of the shell, the incentive package and the utility's role, which is more than the public record usually yields for a corporate captive site.
